objectives: Describe four ways to release the energy stored in biomass
Calculate how much sunlight a crop stores and how much of it becomes electricity
Use the carbon-loop model to explain when biomass adds carbon to the air

questions.prompt: A field gets 1,500 kWh/m² of sunlight a year. The crop stores 1 % of it, and a power station turns 30 % of the fuel's heat into electricity. How much electricity does each square metre give a year?
questions.explain: The crop stores 1,500 × 0.01 = 15 kWh as chemical energy, and burning it at 30 % gives 15 × 0.3 = 4.5 kWh of electricity: 0.3 % of the sunlight. 15 kWh is what the plant stores, before the power station's losses.

questions.prompt: Burning 2 tonnes of carbon releases how much carbon dioxide?
questions.explain: Each carbon atom picks up two oxygen atoms from the air, so 12 parts of carbon become 44 parts of CO₂: 2 × 44.009 ÷ 12.011 ≈ 7.3 tonnes. It is not 2 tonnes because the added oxygen has mass too, and 0.55 tonnes comes from turning the ratio upside down.

questions.prompt: In the carbon-loop model each harvest burns 1 tonne of carbon, only 50 % grows back before the next harvest, and nothing is captured. After 10 harvests, how much carbon has each plant added to the air?
questions.explain: Each harvest the biomass plant releases 1 t and regrowth takes back 0.5 t, leaving 0.5 t in the air: 5 t after 10 harvests. Coal's carbon had been out of the air underground, so all 10 t stays; biomass only adds nothing when as much grows back as was burned.

questions.prompt: On the same land, solar panels deliver tens of times more electricity than crops burned for power. Why use biomass at all?
choices: Burning plants releases no carbon dioxide at the chimney
It is a stored fuel that can run when needed, and it can use wastes that would otherwise rot
Plants capture a larger share of sunlight than solar cells do
Energy crops need no land that could otherwise grow food or forest
questions.explain: Biomass earns its place by being storable, so it can run when wind and solar cannot, and by turning residues, manure and food waste into energy. Plants are poor solar collectors, and burning them does release CO₂; the climate question is whether regrowth takes it back.
